info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 5.2: Character and Word Error Rates: Measuring the Machine Passes.

questiontext.text: What do Character Error Rate (CER) and Word Error Rate (WER) measure in document analysis?

generalfeedback.text: CER and WER are normalized edit distances, and understanding the algorithm is what lets you interpret the numbers rather than quote them.

answer.text: Normalized edit distances representing the minimum number of single-unit insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform machine output into a calibrated reference, divided by the reference length.

feedback.text: Correct. CER and WER are normalized edit distances that quantify the minimum cost of transforming a hypothesis into the ground truth.

answer.text: The percentage of pixels in the manuscript image that match the rendered font glyphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Edit distance measures string discrepancies in character and word sequences, not image pixel overlap.

answer.text: The execution speed of the recognition neural network measured in milliseconds per line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER and WER evaluate transcription accuracy, not algorithmic execution latency.

answer.text: The semantic similarity score produced by cosine distance in high-dimensional word embedding vectors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER and WER operate on exact string edit operations, not semantic embedding distances.

questiontext.text: Which edit operations are permitted in the standard formulation of Levenshtein distance, and how is transposition handled?

generalfeedback.text: Levenshtein distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions — and transposition is not one of the permitted operations.

answer.text: Permitted operations are insertion, deletion, and substitution; transposition is not permitted and counts as two operations.

feedback.text: Correct. Standard Levenshtein allows only insertion, deletion, and substitution; swapping adjacent letters (transposition) costs two edits.

answer.text: Permitted operations are insertion, deletion, and transposition; substitution is forbidden.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Substitution is a core operation in standard Levenshtein distance.

answer.text: Transposition is permitted as a single atomic operation with cost 1 in standard Levenshtein.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Single-operation transposition is part of Damerau-Levenshtein distance, not standard Levenshtein distance.

answer.text: All four operations (insertion, deletion, substitution, and transposition) are permitted with fractional costs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard Levenshtein assigns discrete integer unit costs (1) to insertion, deletion, and substitution.

questiontext.text: In the Wagner-Fischer dynamic programming matrix D of dimensions (m+1) × (n+1), what do row 0 and column 0 represent?

generalfeedback.text: The extra row and column represent the empty string, and back-tracing the matrix recovers not just the distance but the exact alignment of errors.

answer.text: The empty string: row 0 represents the cost of building the hypothesis from nothing (insertions), while column 0 represents the cost of reducing the reference to nothing (deletions).

feedback.text: Correct. The extra row and column represent prefixes of length zero, anchoring the dynamic programming recurrence base cases.

answer.text: The header metadata and TEI schema validation checksums.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wagner-Fischer is a general string alignment matrix and contains no XML metadata or checksums.

answer.text: The memory addresses of the Python garbage collector pointers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The matrix entries store accumulated edit costs, not low-level memory pointers.

answer.text: The first line and first column of the physical manuscript page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The matrix indices represent character sequence positions, with index 0 representing the empty string prefix.

questiontext.text: Why must both the reference and hypothesis strings be normalized to Unicode NFC prior to computing edit distance in Python?

generalfeedback.text: WER is the same algorithm over whitespace tokens — and NFC-normalizing both inputs is what stops you measuring encoding difference.

answer.text: Comparing an NFC string against an NFD string will record false-positive edit errors at every polytonic Greek character with combining diacritics.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalizing both inputs to NFC ensures that identical characters share identical byte representations and code point sequences.

answer.text: Python's string equality operator raises a fatal TypeError when comparing unnormalized strings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python compares raw code point sequences without error; unnormalized strings simply fail to match logically.

answer.text: NFC normalization removes all punctuation marks and converts Greek letters to uppercase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NFC preserves character case and diacritics in canonical precomposed form; it does not strip punctuation.

answer.text: Dynamic programming matrices can only allocate memory for single-byte ASCII characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python arrays and strings seamlessly handle 32-bit Unicode code points.

name.text: 05 Question: The Definitions of CER and WER

questiontext.text: Why can the Character Error Rate (CER = [S + D + I] / N) mathematically exceed 100% (1.0)?

generalfeedback.text: CER can exceed 100% because insertions add to the numerator but not the denominator — a rate above 1.0 means substantial hallucination.

answer.text: Insertions (I) are added to the numerator without increasing the reference character denominator (N), so severe hallucinations yield rates above 100%.

feedback.text: Correct. When a model generates long hallucinated sequences from degraded images, the count of insertions can exceed the total reference character length.

answer.text: A floating-point overflow error occurs in the Python arithmetic logic unit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER > 100% is a mathematically valid outcome of the formula when insertions exceed reference length.

answer.text: The denominator N represents the word count rather than the character count.

feedback.text: Incorrect. N in CER is the reference character count; WER uses reference word count.

answer.text: The calculation is invalid unless normalized by the square root of the matrix diagonal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is simply normalized by the reference length N; no matrix root is used.

name.text: 06 Question: The Relationship Between CER and WER

questiontext.text: What does an error profile with low CER (e.g. 4%) and disproportionately high WER (e.g. 25%) typically diagnose?

generalfeedback.text: Low CER with disproportionately high WER means word-boundary failure, not character misreading — diagnose it rather than reporting it flatly.

answer.text: Systemic word-boundary or tokenization failure (such as scriptio continua fusion or line-end hyphenation fractures) where characters are accurate but spaces are misplaced.

feedback.text: Correct. When characters are largely correct but word boundaries are corrupted, errors scatter across many tokens, driving WER up dramatically.

answer.text: The model made catastrophic character recognition errors on every line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Severe character misrecognition would result in a high CER as well as high WER.

answer.text: The dynamic programming script was compiled with an incorrect optimization flag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The disparity reflects real linguistic and tokenization phenomena in the text stream.

answer.text: The transcriber used the wrong font family during visual inspection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font rendering does not affect computed character or word error rates.

name.text: 07 Question: Preparing the Texts for Comparison

questiontext.text: When extracting text streams from TEI XML before computing error rates, why must an editor deliberately select the <abbr> layer rather than stripping all tags indiscriminately?

generalfeedback.text: Preprocessing decisions change the number, so record them — and when stripping markup, choose the or layer deliberately.

answer.text: Indiscriminately stripping all tags concatenates both <abbr> and <expan> into a doubled nonsense string, severely inflating error rates.

feedback.text: Correct. A `` element contains both the manuscript abbreviation and its editorial expansion; stripping tags keeps both strings, producing doubled text.

answer.text: The TEI parser will throw a fatal syntax exception if <expan> is processed by Python.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python string processing does not crash; it extracts both layers unless specifically filtered.

answer.text: The <abbr> tag is encrypted using SHA-256 hashes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI tags are standard plaintext XML elements.

answer.text: Machine learning recognition engines can read only expanded Latin abbreviations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR models read the raw ink on the page, corresponding to the diplomatic `` layer.

questiontext.text: Why must overall folio CER be calculated as a weighted average by line length rather than a simple arithmetic mean of per-line error rates?

generalfeedback.text: Weight the overall rate by line length, and read the per-line distribution — rising error means misalignment, not model failure.

answer.text: An unweighted mean treats very short lines (e.g. 3 characters) and long lines (e.g. 60 characters) equally, skewing the true aggregate error rate.

feedback.text: Correct. Total edit distance divided by total reference characters correctly weights each line by its contribution to the document.

answer.text: Python's standard library does not support arithmetic division on floating-point lists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python easily computes arithmetic means; the issue is mathematical weighting.

answer.text: Weighted averages are required by the ISO 9001 document certification standard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Weighting by length is a basic mathematical necessity for ratio metrics, not an external standard.

answer.text: Line breaks carry negative edit costs in the Levenshtein dynamic programming matrix.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Edit costs are non-negative; line breaks are structural delimiters.

questiontext.text: Why is HTR output line-aligned by construction, whereas Vision-Language Model (VLM) output often requires manual realignment or whole-text evaluation?

generalfeedback.text: HTR output is line-aligned by construction and VLM output often is not — never compare a per-line figure against a whole-text one without saying so.

answer.text: HTR models process segmented line image polygons and export coordinate-bound lines (ALTO/PAGE XML), whereas VLMs often reflow text into continuous prose.

feedback.text: Correct. HTR architectures operate per line image, while VLMs generate open-ended text tokens that frequently lose physical line structure.

answer.text: HTR models are connected directly to the physical scanner hardware during digitization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR models run on digital image files after segmentation, not directly on hardware.

answer.text: VLMs are legally restricted from outputting newline characters by developer safety filters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Safety filters do not restrict whitespace; VLMs simply lack native line-segmentation grounding.

answer.text: PAGE XML formats can be parsed only on Linux supercomputing clusters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PAGE XML is an open XML format parsable by standard XML tools on any operating system.

name.text: 10 Question: Computing Against Both Ground Truths

questiontext.text: What is revealed by calculating a model's CER against both the original ground truth (gt-f42r) and the double-keyed consensus (gt-f42r-consensus)?

generalfeedback.text: Measuring against both ground truths quantifies how much of Week 4's 'machine error' was yours — and only the tags make it retrievable.

answer.text: The difference between the two scores quantifies how much of Week 4's measured 'machine error' was actually human reference error.

feedback.text: Correct. Comparing scores against uncalibrated and calibrated baselines isolates the proportion of error caused by flaws in the initial human ground truth.

answer.text: It determines whether the Git repository index needs to be rebuilt with garbage collection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Error rate benchmarking evaluates transcription accuracy, not Git index maintenance.

answer.text: It proves that the HTR model had overfitted to the validation split.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Measuring against two ground truths measures reference accuracy, not model overfitting.

answer.text: It converts character error rates into word error rates automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER and WER are computed on different token units, not converted via reference comparisons.

name.text: 11 Question: Interpreting the Numbers Against Thresholds

questiontext.text: According to established document analysis benchmarks (AlKendi et al., 2024), what operational threshold marks a recognition model as a net economic loss?

generalfeedback.text: Above 15% CER a tool is a net loss, not slow help — the threshold converts a quality judgement into a decision.

answer.text: Above 15% CER, where the time and cognitive load of post-correction exceed the effort required to transcribe from scratch.

feedback.text: Correct. When CER exceeds roughly 15%, correcting noisy machine predictions is slower and more mentally taxing than fresh manual transcription.

answer.text: Above 1% CER, which causes immediate failure in commercial OCR engines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 1% to 5% CER is considered excellent and highly usable with minimal post-correction.

answer.text: Above 50% CER, because lower rates can always be corrected instantaneously by regular expressions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regular expressions cannot fix complex graphemic noise, and 15% is the recognized economic threshold.

answer.text: Above 5% CER, which invalidates all TEI schema validation rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation checks XML markup validity, completely independent of text stream CER values.

name.text: 12 Question: Why the Number Is Not Enough

questiontext.text: What did Levchenko's (2024) benchmark on 18th-century Russian demonstrate regarding aggregate CER and diplomatic fidelity?

generalfeedback.text: A model can score better on CER while destroying diplomatic fidelity — compute fidelity measures alongside the error rate.

answer.text: A model can achieve a low CER (e.g. GPT-4o at 9.23%) while destroying diplomatic fidelity by hallucinating anachronistic archaic characters, whereas a higher-CER HTR model never fabricated graphemes.

feedback.text: Correct. Aggregate CER weights all edits equally, concealing severe qualitative failures such as temporal hallucination and fabricated historical orthography.

answer.text: PyLaia models are incapable of processing Cyrillic script encodings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PyLaia processed the Cyrillic scripts; the finding was about graphemic fidelity versus statistical hallucination.

answer.text: Language models always produce higher CER than line-based HTR models across all historical corpora.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GPT-4o achieved a lower numerical CER (9.23% vs 26.93%), but introduced rampant anachronistic insertions.

answer.text: Historical Russian manuscripts can be transcribed only using monotonic Greek fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The study evaluated Russian Cyrillic historical orthography, not Greek fonts.

questiontext.text: In an error audit typology, why are 'plausible wrong words' generated by language models more hazardous than 'impossible character sequences' produced by HTR?

generalfeedback.text: Categorized errors identify systematic bias; an aggregate rate cannot — and plausible wrong words are the ones post-correction will miss.

answer.text: Plausible wrong words fit the syntactic and semantic context smoothly, making them easy for human proofreaders to miss during post-correction.

feedback.text: Correct. An impossible sequence is immediately obvious to an editor, whereas a contextually plausible hallucination slips past reading checks silently.

answer.text: Plausible wrong words crash the Python XML parser during entity expansion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers process any valid Unicode characters regardless of word plausibility.

answer.text: Impossible character sequences automatically corrupt Git branch pointers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text content has no effect on Git internal branch pointers.

answer.text: Plausible wrong words always double the measured Word Error Rate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any wrong word counts as one error in WER; the hazard is cognitive oversight during proofreading.

name.text: 14 Question: Why Error Rates Matter Downstream

questiontext.text: Why does Named Entity Recognition (NER) fail catastrophically (F-score dropping from 90% to 60% as WER rises from 1% to 7%) on noisy transcriptions?

generalfeedback.text: NER collapses from 90% to 60% F-score as WER goes from 1% to 7%, because proper names have no redundancy to recover from.

answer.text: Named entities have low textual redundancy, so a single corrupted character invalidates the entire proper noun, and entities are disproportionately out-of-vocabulary.

feedback.text: Correct. Common words are recoverable from context and repetition, but proper names lack redundancy and are lost to indexing when corrupted.

answer.text: NER algorithms require uncompressed TIFF images to locate proper names.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NER operates on extracted text streams, not raster images.

answer.text: Part-of-speech taggers refuse to process texts with Word Error Rates above 2%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. POS taggers degrade roughly linearly; NER collapses non-linearly due to lack of entity redundancy.

answer.text: Named entities in Greek manuscripts were written exclusively in invisible ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical named entities are standard ink text, but linguistically unique and vulnerable to recognition noise.

questiontext.text: What critical safeguard must be enforced when applying sequence-to-sequence transformers (e.g. ByT5) for pre-editorial normalization of historical text?

generalfeedback.text: Automated normalization works under strict constraints — unexpanded proper names, human review of noisy spans — and erases dialectal evidence without them.

answer.text: Enforce strict constraints so abbreviations representing proper names remain unexpanded and continuous spans of severe noise are flagged for human review rather than hallucinated over.

feedback.text: Correct. Without strict constraints, seq2seq models erase dialectal variants and fabricate coherent text over illegible gaps, destroying evidence.

answer.text: Disable all GPU acceleration to prevent floating-point rounding errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization constraints govern model generation behavior, not hardware execution.

answer.text: Convert all historical Greek text into modern French before processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pre-editorial normalization operates within the historical source language.

answer.text: Require the model to replace all medieval abbreviations with Latin numeric digits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization regularizes graphemic forms (e.g. ramist letters, minims), not numerical replacement.

questiontext.text: In the Reconciliation Audit Report, why do XML structural errors take precedence in severity over typographical character errors?

generalfeedback.text: The audit report has five required components, and structural errors take precedence over typographical ones in reporting.

answer.text: A structural error (such as an unclosed element or broken hierarchy) compromises the entire Document Object Model, rendering the file unparseable by downstream tools.

feedback.text: Correct. Structural errors break XML parsing and invalidate downstream processing pipelines, whereas typographical errors are localized to character positions.

answer.text: Structural errors result in automatic deletion of the Git repository on remote servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks file blobs regardless of XML validity.

answer.text: Typographical errors are legally classified as copyright violations in digital libraries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Typographical errors are simple transcription mistakes, not legal violations.

answer.text: TEI schemas cannot validate files that contain character substitutions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validators verify markup element grammar, ignoring character substitution errors in text content.

name.text: 17 Question: Writing Component 1: Ground Truth Validation

questiontext.text: What must Component 1 of the Reconciliation Audit Report transparently disclose regarding single-author double-keying?

generalfeedback.text: Component 1 lets a reader judge how much confidence your reference deserves — including the limitation of self-double-keying.

answer.text: The limitation of correlated error: self-double-keying cannot catch systematic palaeographical misunderstandings shared across both passes.

feedback.text: Correct. Honest scholarship demands acknowledging the methodological limitation of single-transcriber double-keying in the audit report.

answer.text: A certification that the student's transcription achieved 100.000% mathematical perfection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly reports document empirical metrics and limitations, not unsubstantiated claims of perfection.

answer.text: The serial number of the monitor hardware used during transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware serial numbers are irrelevant to methodological validation.

answer.text: A legal waiver transferring copyright of the manuscript to the university.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground truth validation concerns transcription methodology and agreement reliability, not copyright transfers.

name.text: 18 Question: Writing Component 2: Error Rate Benchmarking

questiontext.text: Why must Component 2 of the audit report explicitly state all preprocessing operations (e.g. whitespace collapsing, case handling, Unicode normalization)?

generalfeedback.text: Report preprocessing, the per-line distribution, and the CER-to-WER relationship — an aggregate alone is neither reproducible nor diagnostic.

answer.text: Preprocessing decisions directly alter edit distance calculations; without stating them, reported error rates are neither comparable nor reproducible.

feedback.text: Correct. A CER calculated with punctuation stripped or case folded differs from a strict calculation; reproducibility requires full preprocessing disclosure.

answer.text: Preprocessing commands must be re-executed in real time by the Moodle grading plugin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Moodle does not execute preprocessing commands; reporting ensures human and scientific reproducibility.

answer.text: Unstated preprocessing causes XML files to fail RelaxNG schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation tests XML grammar, not the preprocessing parameters used in benchmark scripts.

answer.text: Python requires preprocessing metadata in the docstring to compute Levenshtein distance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms compute distances purely from the string inputs provided in memory.

name.text: 19 Question: Writing Components 3 and 4: Typology and Structure

questiontext.text: Why is identifying systematic bias (e.g. recurring confusion of a specific letter pair in 11 of 14 cases) more valuable than reporting random typographical slips?

generalfeedback.text: Systematic errors are more serious and more tractable than random ones — and structural failure takes precedence over typographical error.

answer.text: Systematic biases reveal specific model limitations that can be rectified through targeted training data or rule-based normalization parameters.

feedback.text: Correct. Distinguishing systematic bias from random slips enables actionable improvements in fine-tuning and post-correction workflows.

answer.text: Systematic biases automatically disqualify a digital edition from being deposited in library archives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identifying biases is a standard step in refining editions and models.

answer.text: Random slips cannot be recorded in Markdown tables due to formatting constraints.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Markdown tables can format any text data; the value lies in analytical diagnosis.

answer.text: Systematic errors have zero impact on downstream Named Entity Recognition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Systematic errors directly corrupt downstream NLP tools, making their identification essential.

questiontext.text: How does Component 5 of the audit report evaluate a language model's compliance with negative prompting constraints?

generalfeedback.text: Report constraint compliance instruction by instruction — that table measures how far explicit prompting actually constrained the model.

answer.text: By auditing output against each negative constraint (e.g. do not expand abbreviations, do not modernize spelling, do not supply text across gaps) to measure the false-positive rate.

feedback.text: Correct. Component 5 quantitatively audits whether the model obeyed explicit negative constraints or succumbed to unprompted anachronistic normalization.

answer.text: By measuring the GPU temperature during API call execution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware operational telemetry does not evaluate prompt constraint compliance.

answer.text: By verifying that the prompt was translated into 16th-century Early Modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts are evaluated on how effectively they constrained the model on the target manuscript.

answer.text: By checking whether the model API returned an HTTP 404 response code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTTP status codes indicate network connectivity, not linguistic constraint compliance.

questiontext.text: What characterizes a scientifically sound and actionable conclusion in a transcription reconciliation report?

generalfeedback.text: State what you measured, on what material, with what consequence for your edition — a general claim about AI is not a finding.

answer.text: Stating specific measured metrics on a named manuscript witness, identifying exact error concentrations, and providing concrete operational decisions on tool adoption.

feedback.text: Correct. Strong conclusions are grounded in empirical measurements on specific historical materials and provide clear, defensible workflow choices.

answer.text: Making sweeping, unsubstantiated generalizations that artificial intelligence is entirely useless for historical studies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sweeping assertions are unscientific; reports require specific, evidence-based assessments.

answer.text: Claiming that automated models have rendered human palaeographical expertise completely obsolete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Empirical audits demonstrate that human diplomatic expertise is essential for grounding and post-correction.

answer.text: Recommending that all historical manuscripts be transcribed exclusively using speech recognition software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conclusions must logically follow from the experimental findings on the written witness.

questiontext.text: Why is the Git commit history with provenance trailers evaluated as a primary deliverable alongside the TEI XML text?

generalfeedback.text: The commit history with provenance trailers is assessed alongside the text — indistinguishable machine and human commits fail the requirement.

answer.text: It provides an auditable, tamper-evident record proving the independent creation, attribution, and systematic adjudication of all human and machine contributions.

feedback.text: Correct. Provenance trailers and commit histories demonstrate the evidential integrity and scholarly rigor of the entire editorial workflow.

answer.text: Git commit logs are automatically converted into PDF diplomas by university registrar offices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Assessment evaluates scholarly methodology and transparency, not automated diploma generation.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium requires commit logs to assign an ISBN to digital publications.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI guidelines govern encoding; assessment focuses on reproducible research practices.

answer.text: Repositories without commit histories cannot be cloned over SSH network connections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git operates over SSH regardless of commit message content; trailers provide scholarly provenance.

questiontext.text: Why is it essential to create an annotated Git tag (submission-transcription) and push it to the remote repository upon assignment completion?

generalfeedback.text: Tag and push the submitted state — within three weeks of further work it becomes otherwise unrecoverable.

answer.text: Subsequent coursework in Weeks 6–13 will continually modify the repository files, making the submitted state unrecoverable without an immutable tag.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital editions evolve across terms; tagging snapshots the exact submitted milestone so it remains retrievable and assessable.

answer.text: Git servers delete repositories that do not receive a tag within 30 days of creation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git repositories persist indefinitely regardless of tag presence.

answer.text: Tags are required to compress XML files into binary zip archives on GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags are references to specific commits, not file compression tools.

answer.text: Annotated tags automatically grant commercial copyright licenses to the course instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags record release milestones and carry no copyright licensing implications.

name.text: 24 Question: What the Two Weeks Established

questiontext.text: What fundamental thesis did the completed transcription and reconciliation pipeline (Weeks 4 and 5) empirically validate?

generalfeedback.text: You now have measured figures for your own manuscript rather than the literature's account — which is what makes your tool choices defensible.

answer.text: Automated transcription models require a calibrated human diplomatic ground truth, because recognition errors, systematic biases, and hallucinations can be measured only against such a baseline.

feedback.text: Correct. Machine learning models cannot be evaluated or safely utilized without a verified, calibrated human diplomatic reference.

answer.text: Machine transcription can completely bypass human verification if prompts are sufficiently detailed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The two weeks demonstrated that unconstrained models hallucinate and fail on out-of-vocabulary manuscript forms.

answer.text: Character error rates are purely theoretical numbers with no practical impact on digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Error rates dictate post-correction economics and determine downstream NLP validity.

answer.text: Manual double-keying is obsolete and should never be used in scholarly digital humanities projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying remains the gold standard for calibrating ground truth references.

questiontext.text: If a student discovers that VLM output could not be aligned line-by-line due to text reflowing, what is the required reporting procedure?

generalfeedback.text: State what could not be computed as a limitation rather than omitting it — a silent gap is worse than a reported one.

answer.text: Report whole-text error figures and explicitly state the alignment limitation in the audit report rather than omitting the data silently.

feedback.text: Correct. Openly reporting methodological constraints and limitations is a hallmark of rigorous scholarly reporting.

answer.text: Invent synthetic line breaks randomly without consulting the manuscript image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fabricating data destroys the integrity of the measurement.

answer.text: Delete the VLM pass entirely and pretend the experiment was never conducted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting failed experiments creates publication bias and conceals important findings.

answer.text: Abort the course and request an incomplete grade from the academic dean.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Methodological limitations are normal and should simply be transparently documented.

questiontext.text: What happens if an editor computes CER on a TEI XML fragment containing <choice><abbr>θς</abbr><expan>θεός</expan></choice> by stripping tags with a naive regular expression?

generalfeedback.text: Stripping all tags concatenates and into nonsense — extract one layer consistently on both sides.

answer.text: The extracted text becomes θςθεός (concatenating abbreviation and expansion), creating an artificial mismatch that inflates the error rate.

feedback.text: Correct. Naive tag stripping joins alternative text layers together, producing doubled nonsense words that distort edit distance.

answer.text: The regular expression engine causes a stack overflow and crashes the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Simple regex operations execute quickly; the error is logical (extracting concatenated text).

answer.text: The XML file is automatically converted into an uncompressed audio WAV recording.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex text filtering operates strictly on string characters.

answer.text: The Python compiler ignores the string and returns a CER of exactly 0.00%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The string is processed, but the resulting concatenated text produces massive false error rates.

name.text: 27 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: Why is the transparent disclosure of methodological limitations (such as single-author double-keying or unaligned machine prose) considered a hallmark of excellent scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: A report that names its own limitations is more trustworthy than one presenting figures without qualification.

answer.text: It establishes intellectual honesty and provides readers with the necessary context to calibrate their confidence in the reported figures.

feedback.text: Correct. Naming limitations distinguishes critical scholarship from unverified assertion, allowing peers to accurately interpret the findings.

answer.text: It guarantees that the student will receive automatic immunity from academic grading rubrics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Academic assessment rewards rigor and honesty, not immunity from criteria.

answer.text: It allows commercial AI vendors to correct their proprietary models free of charge.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly auditing serves academic transparency and research validity, not corporate model tuning.

answer.text: It proves that historical manuscripts are too corrupted for digital processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transparent reporting contextualizes successful processing within realistic boundaries.

questiontext.text: How will the consensus text established today serve the upcoming tasks in Week 6 (Orthographic Normalization)?

generalfeedback.text: Week 6 normalizes as a separate layer over your verified consensus, with Tuesday's hand-recorded rules as Friday's reference.

answer.text: It provides the verified diplomatic base over which regularizations (such as iotacism and <orig>/<reg>) can be built as a distinct, traceable layer.

feedback.text: Correct. Week 6 builds normalization as a separate layer over the consensus text, ensuring regularizations are not entangled with transcription errors.

answer.text: It will be permanently deleted and replaced with a modern printed translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The diplomatic consensus is preserved as the foundation of the digital edition.

answer.text: It will be converted into binary machine code to train autonomous drone navigation systems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The text is used for philological normalization and digital textual editing.

answer.text: It eliminates the need to record any further editorial decisions in Week 6.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 6 introduces explicit normalization rules that build directly upon the consensus text.

questiontext.text: What overarching cyclical pattern connects all subsequent analytical stages (normalization, collation, apparatus, lemmatization) in this course?

generalfeedback.text: Every remaining week repeats this procedure on a different operation — establish a reference by hand, verify it, measure against it.

answer.text: Establish a verified reference by hand, apply automated computational methods, measure the distance between them, categorize errors, and report with limitations stated.

feedback.text: Correct. Every stage repeats the same rigorous scientific cycle: hand-crafted reference, automated execution, empirical measurement, and transparent auditing.

answer.text: Download third-party datasets from the internet, run automated neural scripts, and publish without human review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course emphasizes rigorous human grounding and empirical verification over passive automation.

answer.text: Translate all Greek texts into Latin, format with Microsoft Word, and print on parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The curriculum focuses on digital TEI XML standards and reproducible computational methods.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: What the Numbers Are For

questiontext.text: Why is reporting an isolated error rate number (e.g. 'CER = 5.9%') without its methodological context fundamentally deficient?

generalfeedback.text: A measurement is an argument whose premises are the reference, the preprocessing, and the alignment — reporting a figure without them is assertion, not measurement.

answer.text: A measurement is an argument whose validity depends entirely on its premises: the calibrated reference, preprocessing decisions, alignment methods, and error typology.

feedback.text: Correct. An isolated figure is an unverified assertion; only the surrounding audit report provides the evidentiary basis that makes the measurement meaningful.
